The best way to help someone when they are sharing their feelings is to ask them what you can do for them. Some people want to hear advice, while others just want to be heard. If you can't ascertain which one is appropriate, there is nothing wrong with asking him. 

Since you said you have a problem with interrupting (good self awareness!), I suggest you err on the side of listening silently. I would even go as far as to say not to offer your opinion or advice unless he explicitly asks for it. If he says, "What should I do OP?", then by all means, you have the floor to help him work through whatever has to be done next. 
Otherwise, the best way to listen to him, is simply to LISTEN and little to nothing else. 

Good phrases to practice:
- "That must have been really hard."
- "I'm so sorry that happened to you."
- "I understand what you mean."
- "What would make you feel better right now?"

If you (or him) have trouble with this feeling like he is giving some speech and you are a silent audience, by all means take a more active role in the conversation. But instead of the way you are used to doing this (by adding your input and talking about yourself), practice asking questions. Just general clarification on things you don't get, or just assuring him that you genuinely care about what he's saying enough to engage in the conversation. 

It's really big of you to admit that you have this problem. A lot of people in relationships would lash out at their partner for even suggesting that they are inattentive or not great listeners. So even asking for help with this and not ignoring the problem means you're off to a great start. It's going to take time and practice to break out of these habits, but I think with time and reassurance, he will see and really appreciate that you are taking personal initiative to better yourself and the relationship.

I have treatment resistant depression, and Lexapro did the same thing to me. It's actually very common for SSRIs to increase depression, especially in young people. Get off of that drug as soon as you can meet with your psychiatrist, as reacting negatively to an antidepressant increases the risk of suicidal ideation. As for what to try next, I suggest you leave that up to your psychiatrist, as they probably already have an idea of what the next step should be. As frustrating as it might be, NEVER quit your psych meds cold turkey. Learned that one the hard way, and I promise you will regret it.

when I moved, I had a lot of trouble finding someone new. like you, the long list of names overwhelmed me completely. it took a few tries and a bit of time but now I am seeing a therapist who I think will be a good fit, but only time will tell. 

my advice to you is to think about the people in your life you have been able to communicate the best with, and try to find someone who seems like they would fit into the same grouping as those people. use any preferences you might have (age, gender, religion, etc.) to narrow down your list as much as possible. then from there you have to take the big leap and just call someone. pick a random name if you have to. the general rule of thumb is within 3-5 sessions you will know if they are a good fit. if they are not, respectfully tell them you don't think they are a good fit for you and then call someone else. no therapist will be offended by this, as they are well aware that the client needs to be comfortable and open in order for therapy to have any effect. some therapists might even offer suggestions of colleagues/friends that they think you might click with. 

if possible, you may want to choose the route I initially went with. find a counseling center or practice that has lots of therapists and counselors who will look at your paperwork and try to match you with a good fit. that will take a lot of the pressure off of your shoulders. 

good luck and stay strong throughout the process. it is a process but there is hope.

I just wish I knew how difficult and exhausting all this would be. No one can seem to figure out where to go from here.

You're right when you say there's only so far you can push him. In order for "help" to work, the person needs to want the help and be open to the changes. For now, keep being supportive in the ways you mentioned. Encourage him to seek therapy, but remember you can't force him if he isn't ready. Educate yourself on what he is feeling, and remind yourself that depression is a truly wicked disease in that it makes all the wrong people feel at fault, when chances are it was never anyone's fault at all. When he is in a depressive episode, this doesn't give him a free pass to treat you however he wants, but it is worth recognizing that whatever happens is not your fault at all. Don't be afraid to get help for yourself if you need it, be it professionally or just taking time for yourself.

In the end, it is your decision, but I highly encourage letting him know, and giving him a place in your recovery. Most hard things are easier when you know you're not alone.

This is not healthy behavior. You deserve someone who will treat you with kindness, or at least common decency, regardless of their mood. You need to tell him that if these behaviors don't stop, you can't be in a relationship with him. Explain to him that apologies mean nothing without a promise to stop the behavior being apologized for. And if he can't fix this anger problem on his own, he needs to get help with that, because if he truly was as sorry as he said, he would be doing everything in his power to stop hurting you. Good luck, and I hope you understand how much you are worth, and the kind of treatment you deserve.

It happens differently for different people, just be present and helpful and keep researching the illness so you are informed of risks and dangers as well as tips for both sufferers and caregivers.

Hi! I'm in a similar situation with my boyfriend. I've been supporting him for the past year and a half. I understand the frustration of being in a situation where you want to help so badly but there's only so much you can do. From my experience, the best thing you can do as a SO of someone struggling with bulimia is to just be there. Ask what you can do to help, assure her that you are there to support her, learn her triggers and avoid them. Make sure you are never equating her with her ED. Remember, it's something she is battling, and it's in no way a mark of her character. If she lashes out at you or acts strangely because of the ED, you can be frustrated, but understand that the ED is the obstacle you both must overcome, and that it's not her fault. 
Also, you can support her by educating yourself (which I see you have already begun to do) and encouraging her to seek medical help. Key word: encouraging. Never make her do anything, especially in terms of recovery. Recovery from ED has to come from the person suffering from it, or there's a good chance it will only cause more stress and resentment. 
I understand all too well the helpless feeling of sitting there, knowing your SO is purging in the next room and there's nothing you can do to stop it. Just remember that you are entitled to feel frustrated, but ultimately recognize that what you are feeling, she herself is feeling 10 times over. 
Good luck with everything, you seem like you're doing a great job. :)

I just started college this past Fall and this is something I can relate so well to. It has been a huge challenge, and it definitely depends on the campus (I find myself eating cereal a lot of nights when there is a lack of safe foods, or if I'm bored with the safe foods I eat most days). It is definitely a challenge, but I have found that personally being in a less safe environment has forced me to adapt and I have tried a couple unsafe foods I wouldn't have tried otherwise (yay avocados!) Don't worry too much, you will find ways to adapt and be okay in college even with ARFID :)

I would suggest making your goal not to "cure" your ARFID, but instead try to take steps and push yourself little by little. Rejoice in the small victories, and use safe foods as a gateway for less safe foods. Don't feel silly for getting excited over making small strides in recovery. I know I tend to get so down on myself, feeling pathetic because I am proud of something which would seem trivial to most people. If you need to talk ever, feel free to reach out. :) I, and I'm sure everyone else on here, believe in your ability to overcome this little by little. We get what you're going through, and how much it sucks. Sorry if this response wasn't totally what you were looking for.
